## Concept

### Pitch

Suspense keeps itself up to date: it looks for a newer edge release, downloads it in the background, and puts it in place of its own binary when it restarts, so the newest build is only a restart away.

### Shape

#### Description

Updates come from the edge releases, as the [EdgeReleasesScope](../edge-releases/index.md#edge-releases-scope) says, published in the GitHub repository the running build was published from, which it knows because that is baked into it. Only such a build updates itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, never looks for an update, never downloads one, and never replaces its binary, and the Updates section says why.

#### Checking

A check asks GitHub's releases API for the repository's releases, pre-releases included, and takes the one with the highest version `0.1.N`, comparing N as a number, never as text. It is newer only when its N is greater than the running build's; an older or equal one is never taken, so an update never goes back. A release without the asset for the running platform is passed over for the newest one that has it.
Suspense checks a few seconds after it starts, and then every 6 hours while it runs, in the background, never holding up anything else, and only while "Check for updates automatically" is on, as it is until turned off. That choice is remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says. Check for updates, in the Updates section, checks straight away, whether it is on or not. A check that can't be made, as with no network or GitHub refusing it, is quiet when automatic, trying again at the next, and says why when asked for.

#### Downloading

A newer release found is downloaded straight away, in the background, taking the asset for the platform and architecture running, `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`, or `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`. It is checked against the size GitHub gives for it, and against its SHA-256 digest where GitHub gives one, and one that doesn't match is thrown away and never used. The binary is taken out of the archive and staged beside the running binary, in the same directory, so it can be put in place by a rename, marked executable where the platform has such a mark. One download runs at a time; a newer release found while one is staged replaces it. A download that fails says so in the Updates section, and is tried again at the next check.
Where the running binary's directory can't be written, nothing is downloaded, and the Updates section says that Suspense can't update itself there, with the directory, and a link to the release's page, opened in the browser, so it can be updated by hand.

#### Restarting

Once an update is staged, a notification says "Suspense 0.1.N is ready", with a Restart button and a Later button. The Updates section says the same, with a Restart button, for as long as it stays staged. Later only closes the notification; the update stays staged, and is put in place whenever Suspense next quits.
Restart quits as quitting does, as the [MainWindowScope](../application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope) says, asking first while work is running, and doing nothing more if the quit is cancelled, then starts Suspense again from the same path once the update is in place. However Suspense quits, a staged update is put in place as it does: the staged binary is renamed over the running one, the running one renamed aside first where the platform won't replace a running binary, as on Windows. The binary set aside is deleted at the next launch. An update left staged by a quit that never finished, as a crash, is put in place at the next launch, before anything else, and takes effect at the launch after, the Updates section saying a restart finishes it.
Putting an update in place never leaves Suspense without a binary: a step that fails puts back the binary that was there, and the Updates section says why it couldn't update.

#### Updates Section

The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) has an "Updates" section. It says the running version, as "Suspense 0.1.42", and where it can't update itself, as for a build made elsewhere, why, and offers nothing else. Otherwise it shows a checkbox reading "Check for updates automatically", a "Check for updates" button, disabled while a check or download is under way, and a line saying where things stand: "Checking for updates…", "Suspense is up to date", checked when, as "Checked 5 minutes ago", "Downloading 0.1.N…" with how much has come, "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" with a Restart button, or, in the theme's error colour, why the last check, download, or update failed.
## Concept

### Pitch

Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

### Shape

#### Description

A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository, `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push, for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

#### Version

An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds, counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.
The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the application knows its own version, and so is the repository it is published from, as `owner/name`, which marks it as an edge build that can update itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it, and no repository.

#### Builds

The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

- Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
- Windows, x86_64
- macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no console of its own, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says.
The code compiles, its tests included, on each of the three platforms, with no compiler warnings on any of them. What differs between platforms, as a system call whose signature differs between Linux and macOS, or an import only one platform uses, is written for each platform it builds on, and gated to the platforms that use it, so nothing is unused or mistyped on another. No deprecated function is called where its replacement is available. Each job denies warnings in its build and its tests, so a warning fails the job, and no edge release is published, as for an error. A build script's own notes, as one saying where the default prompts were taken from, are not compiler warnings, and don't fail it.
Every test passes on each of the three platforms, on a fresh GitHub-hosted runner, every time, run in parallel as `cargo test` runs them, in any order. A test asks for what the platform it runs on does, never what one platform does:

- A shortcut is pressed as the platform binds it, as the application binds it there, <Cmd> on macOS where <Ctrl> elsewhere, as <Cmd+Shift+Enter> opening the chat input's send menu on macOS, so a test that opens a menu, sends, or saves with a keystroke does so on every platform.
- A path is built with the platform's own separators and compared as the platform compares paths, never written as a literal with `/` and compared as text, and line endings are compared without regard to `\r\n` or `\n`.
- Nothing a test needs is taken from the machine: not piton, Podman, a harness, a network, the user's home or config directories, or a display's scale. What it needs, it makes or fakes in a temporary directory of its own, removed when it ends, so the runners, which have no piton or Podman, run it as a developer's machine does. Git, which every runner has, is the one exception, configured with a name and email for the test alone.
- A test that waits on something running in the background waits for it to happen, with a timeout generous enough for the slowest runner, never for a fixed time.
- A test finds what it clicks or reads by the element ids the interface gives it, kept in step with the interface: an id a test uses is one the interface has, under the scope it is looked for in, in the frame it is looked for, as a menu's options once the menu is open.

#### Publishing

Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash, linked to the commit, and its message's first line.
Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary alone, named for the version and the platform:

- `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
- `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
- `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

The binaries are not signed or notarized.
If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit, so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing more for it and succeeds.
Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents, and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its own.

I couldn't find the actual bug from here. This step runs in a container that can't see the code, and Suspense has no update log yet. So I tightened the spec where self-update most often breaks silently, and added a log and diagnostics so the next failure is visible. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 81 files, and the new sections are in the refreshed reference.

**Likeliest causes, worth checking first in the code step:**
1. **Version or repository not baked into the edge build.** If the workflow doesn't pass them in, the build never updates, or thinks it's version 0.1.0 and updates again on every launch.
2. **No User-Agent on GitHub requests.** GitHub refuses requests without one.
3. **Downloading the asset without following GitHub's redirect.**
4. **Leaving the renamed-aside binary on Windows** while the old process is still exiting.

## What changed in the spec

**Edge releases** (`.claude/reference/scope/edge-releases/index.md#version`)
- The workflow must pass the version and `owner/name` to every platform's build. A build never falls back to Cargo.toml's version or to no repository on the runner.
- `suspense --version` prints, for example, "Suspense 0.1.42 (owner/name)" or "Suspense 0.1.0 (development build)", and exits without opening a window. On Windows it writes to standard output even though the app has no console.
- Each job runs the binary it built with `--version` before archiving it, and fails if the output doesn't match what it was given. So no edge release can ship a binary that can't update itself or that keeps updating.

**Self-update** (`.claude/reference/scope/self-update/index.md`)
- **`#requests`:**
  - Every request sends a `Suspense/0.1.N` User-Agent and `Accept: application/vnd.github+json`.
  - The releases list is fetched 100 to a page, ignoring drafts and tags not of the form `v0.1.N`.
  - Assets are downloaded from `browser_download_url`, following redirects, and the `sha256:` digest is compared ignoring case.
  - When GitHub's rate limit is hit, the message names the reset time and automatic checks wait until then. Any other refusal shows GitHub's status and message.
- **`#after-update`:**
  - The launch after an update confirms the running version matches what was staged, and shows "Updated to Suspense 0.1.N".
  - If it doesn't match, the Updates section reports an error and that release is never put in place again automatically, so an update can't loop. Check for updates by hand still tries it.
  - On Windows, the set-aside binary is deleted at a later launch if it can't be deleted yet.
  - A staged binary that is no newer than the running one is deleted.
- **`#diagnostics`:**
  - An `updates.log` (last 1,000 lines) in Suspense's data directory records every check, download, staging, swap and launch confirmation, with full errors.
  - A "Details" disclosure in the Updates section shows the running version, the repository or that this isn't an edge build, the binary's path and whether it can be written, the last check and newest release found, and what's staged.
  - Details has "Show log" and "Copy" buttons for bug reports.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791134228-DebugSelfUpdate.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `EdgeReleasesScope`: `#version`, for `edge.yml` and the `--version` flag and its check.
- `SelfUpdateScope`: `#requests`, `#after-update`, `#diagnostics`, plus the existing `#checking`, `#downloading` and `#restarting`, read against the code to find what differs.
- `UserPreferencesScope`: where the log goes.
- `OpenFileScope`: how Show log opens it.
